LS.L5.PSW.T01.title: Positive self-concept formation
LS.L5.PSW.T01.description: Influence of adults and peers on self-concept, personal successes as contributors to a positive self-concept, action plan for continued positive self-concept formation.
LS.L5.PSW.T01.recovery_strategy: Affirm that self-concept grows from many small wins and from kind voices around us. Help the learner identify supportive people and one strength they can build on.

questions.question: What is 'self-concept'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Let's start with the words. What does 'self-concept' mean?
options: The way you see and think about yourself
The time you go to bed
questions.expected: The way you see and think about yourself
questions.memo: Self-concept is your inner picture of yourself — your strengths, your worth, what you can do. It grows over time.

questions.question: A POSITIVE self-concept means you mostly think:
questions.ruby_prompt: Someone with a positive self-concept mostly thinks what about themselves?
options: 'I am valuable and I can learn and grow.'
'I am useless and can't do anything.'
questions.expected: 'I am valuable and I can learn and grow.'
questions.memo: Positive self-concept = realistic and kind to yourself. Not bragging, not putting yourself down — just steady belief in your worth and growth.

questions.question: Which adults can SHAPE a child's self-concept?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which adults shape how a child sees themselves?
options: Parents, teachers, family members and caregivers
questions.expected: Parents, teachers, family members and caregivers
questions.memo: The grown-ups closest to us — parents, teachers, family — have the biggest influence on our self-concept, especially when we're young.

questions.question: True or false: Friends and peers can also affect how you see yourself.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Friends and peers also affect how you see yourself.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — friends shape our self-concept too. Kind friends help us grow; unkind ones can hurt our self-image. Choose friends carefully.

questions.question: Thandi did well at her school athletics. How does this affect her self-concept?
questions.ruby_prompt: Thandi did really well at school athletics. How does this affect her self-concept?
options: It builds her positive self-concept — she sees herself as capable
questions.expected: It builds her positive self-concept — she sees herself as capable
questions.memo: Real successes — small or big — are the building blocks of a healthy self-concept. They give us proof we can do things.

questions.question: Which of these is a 'personal success' that builds self-concept?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a personal success that builds your self-concept?
options: Finishing a hard piece of homework on my own
questions.expected: Finishing a hard piece of homework on my own
questions.memo: Personal successes are things YOU did with effort — they grow your sense that you can. Watching TV doesn't change your self-view.

questions.question: When an adult says, 'I'm proud of you for trying,' it usually:
questions.ruby_prompt: When an adult says 'I'm proud of you for trying,' what does that usually do for a child?
options: Helps the child see themselves as someone who can keep trying
questions.expected: Helps the child see themselves as someone who can keep trying
questions.memo: Praise for EFFORT (not just results) builds a strong self-concept. It tells the child: trying is what matters, and I am someone who tries.

questions.question: Sipho's friends keep telling him he is bad at maths. How might this affect him?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho's friends keep telling him he is bad at maths. How might this affect him over time?
options: He may start to believe it and stop trying — even though it's not the truth
He will get better at maths instantly
questions.expected: He may start to believe it and stop trying — even though it's not the truth
questions.memo: What people repeat to us, we often start to believe. This is why unkind friends hurt self-concept. Sipho needs voices that tell him the truth: he CAN learn maths.

questions.question: What's an 'action plan' for self-concept?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's an 'action plan' for building your self-concept?
options: A simple list of small steps to grow your strengths and confidence
questions.expected: A simple list of small steps to grow your strengths and confidence
questions.memo: An action plan is real and small: practise reading 10 minutes a day; ask one new person to play this week. Self-concept grows through action, not wishing.

questions.question: Put these in order for making a small action plan to build your self-concept.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order — making a small action plan to build your self-concept.
options: Notice one strength or area you want to grow
Choose one small step you can take this week
Do the step and notice how you feel afterwards
questions.expected: Notice one strength or area you want to grow,Choose one small step you can take this week,Do the step and notice how you feel afterwards,Plan the next step
questions.memo: Notice → step → reflect → next step. Self-concept builds through tiny repeated wins, not one big leap.

questions.question: Tell me one thing you did well recently.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing you did well recently that you feel good about.
questions.expected: I helped my younger brother with his homework
questions.memo: Good answers: any real success — finished a task, learned a new skill, helped someone, controlled my temper, told the truth. All of these build self-concept.

questions.question: True or false: Self-concept can grow over time.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Self-concept can grow stronger over time.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — self-concept is not fixed. With supportive people and real successes, it grows. With unkind voices, it can shrink — but that can be turned around.

questions.question: Karabo failed a test. The healthiest response is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo failed a test. What's the healthiest response for her self-concept?
options: 'I didn't do well this time. I will study more for next time.'
questions.expected: 'I didn't do well this time. I will study more for next time.'
questions.memo: A healthy self-concept survives failure — because failing one test isn't the same as being a failure. Learners with strong self-concept bounce back.

questions.question: Which is a way ADULTS can damage a child's self-concept?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these damages a child's self-concept?
options: Calling them names or comparing them harshly to others
questions.expected: Calling them names or comparing them harshly to others
questions.memo: Name-calling and comparison teach children to see themselves as 'less than'. Adults' words leave deep marks — good and bad.

questions.question: Which sentence shows a positive self-concept?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which sentence shows a positive self-concept?
options: 'I am learning and growing every day.'
questions.expected: 'I am learning and growing every day.'
questions.memo: Positive self-concept is humble AND confident at the same time — 'I matter, I'm growing, and so are others.'

questions.question: Mpho can't draw well yet, but she wants to. What action plan would help?
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho wants to get better at drawing. What action plan would help build her self-concept around art?
options: Draw a small picture each day for two weeks and notice progress
Compare every drawing to a master artist
questions.expected: Draw a small picture each day for two weeks and notice progress
questions.memo: Daily small effort + noticing progress = self-concept growth. Comparing yourself to experts only crushes you.

questions.question: Why is comparing yourself to others harmful?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does comparing yourself to other people often hurt your self-concept?
options: Each person has different gifts and different starting points
questions.expected: Each person has different gifts and different starting points
questions.memo: Comparison is unfair: you're measuring your inside against someone else's outside. Compare yourself to your past self instead — are you growing?

questions.question: Which of these helps a child build a strong self-concept at home?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these helps a child build self-concept at home?
options: Adults who listen, praise effort, and let them try things
Being told they can't do things
questions.expected: Adults who listen, praise effort, and let them try things
questions.memo: A child who is heard and supported grows confident. Letting them try (and sometimes fail) is part of that.

questions.question: True or false: A child can build self-concept even if some adults around them are harsh.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: A child can still build a positive self-concept even if some adults around them are harsh.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — even one kind adult, one supportive teacher, one good friend can help a child build self-concept. Hold onto the supportive voices.

questions.question: Which is the BEST starting place to grow your self-concept?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the best starting place to grow your self-concept?
options: Notice one thing you already do well, and build on it with practice
Wait for someone to save you
questions.expected: Notice one thing you already do well, and build on it with practice
questions.memo: Self-concept grows from REAL strengths. Find one. Practise it. Notice progress. Pick the next one. That's the recipe.

LS.L5.PSW.T02.title: Giving and receiving feedback
LS.L5.PSW.T02.description: Appropriate ways of giving positive and negative feedback to peers; appropriate ways of receiving feedback from peers and adults.
LS.L5.PSW.T02.recovery_strategy: Feedback is a gift, even when it stings. Help the learner separate the message from the messenger and practise calm responses.

questions.question: What is 'feedback'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is feedback?
options: Information someone gives you about how you did something
questions.expected: Information someone gives you about how you did something
questions.memo: Feedback tells you what went well or what could be better. It helps you grow.

questions.question: Which is an example of POSITIVE feedback?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is an example of positive feedback?
options: 'I really like how you helped Lebo today.'
questions.expected: 'I really like how you helped Lebo today.'
questions.memo: Positive feedback names the good thing specifically. It's encouraging and tells the person what to keep doing.

questions.question: Which is an example of HELPFUL negative feedback?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is an example of helpful negative feedback — feedback that points out something to fix, but in a kind way?
options: 'Your handwriting is hard to read here — try writing a bit bigger next time.'
questions.expected: 'Your handwriting is hard to read here — try writing a bit bigger next time.'
questions.memo: Helpful negative feedback points out the issue AND offers a way forward. Insults are not feedback.

questions.question: When giving feedback, you should focus on:
questions.ruby_prompt: When giving feedback, what should you focus on?
options: The work or action — not the whole person
Other people they should be like
questions.expected: The work or action — not the whole person
questions.memo: Feedback is about what someone DID, not who they ARE. 'Your essay needs more detail' — not 'you are bad at writing'.

questions.question: True or false: Telling someone exactly what they did wrong is the same as being mean.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Telling someone what they did wrong is the same as being mean.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: They are not the same. Kind, specific feedback HELPS people. Insults hurt. The difference is in how it's said and why.

questions.question: Which is the BEST way to give feedback to a friend?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the best way to give feedback to a friend?
options: In private, kindly, and naming both what worked and what to improve
In front of everyone to shame them
questions.expected: In private, kindly, and naming both what worked and what to improve
questions.memo: Private + kind + specific + balanced (good AND areas to grow) = feedback your friend can actually use.

questions.question: Your teacher tells you your essay needs more detail. The best response is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Your teacher says your essay needs more detail. What's the best response?
options: Say thanks, ask 'where exactly?', and try again
Tell the teacher she is wrong
Cry and refuse to write again
questions.expected: Say thanks, ask 'where exactly?', and try again
questions.memo: Receiving feedback well = listen, accept, ask questions, act on it. That is how learners grow.

questions.question: Sipho's classmate says, 'Your project is great but the picture is upside down.' Sipho should:
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho's classmate says, 'Your project is great but the picture is upside down.' What's the best response?
options: 'Thanks for noticing! Let me fix it.'
questions.expected: 'Thanks for noticing! Let me fix it.'
questions.memo: A small fix saves him from a bigger embarrassment. The classmate was actually being helpful — Sipho's friend, not enemy.

questions.question: True or false: You can disagree with feedback after thinking about it.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: You can disagree with feedback after thinking about it.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — not all feedback is right. After listening calmly, you can decide what to act on. But hear it first.

questions.question: What's a calm response when feedback hurts a little?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a calm response when feedback hurts a little?
options: Breathe, thank them, and think about it later
Burst into tears in front of everyone
questions.expected: Breathe, thank them, and think about it later
questions.memo: Hard feedback stings — that's normal. Buying time with a calm 'thanks, let me think' protects the relationship AND you.

questions.question: Put these in order for giving feedback to a classmate.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order for giving good feedback to a classmate.
options: Find a kind way to say what could improve
Say both — what's good first, then the improvement
questions.expected: Notice what works well,Find a kind way to say what could improve,Say both — what's good first, then the improvement,Ask if they have questions
questions.memo: Notice, soften the improvement, share both, check in. This 'sandwich' of feedback is widely used because it lands well.

questions.question: Which is NOT feedback — it's just rude?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is not feedback — it's just rude?
options: 'Your maths working is missing a step here.'
'I think your story would be even better with one more example.'
questions.expected: 'You're horrible.'
questions.memo: 'You're horrible' attacks the person and offers nothing useful. That's not feedback — it's an insult.

questions.question: Tell me one POSITIVE feedback you could give to a classmate.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me a positive piece of feedback you could give to a classmate today.
questions.expected: I liked how you helped me with my maths today
questions.memo: Good answers: any specific, kind, true compliment about something they DID. Specific is much better than 'you're nice'.

questions.question: Why is it important to RECEIVE feedback well, even when it's negative?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it important to receive feedback well, even when it's negative?
options: Feedback is one of the fastest ways to learn and grow
questions.expected: Feedback is one of the fastest ways to learn and grow
questions.memo: People who can hear feedback grow faster than people who can't. It's a real life skill.

questions.question: Lerato just performed a song. Mpho says, 'I loved the start. The middle was a bit fast — try slower.' This is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato just performed a song. Mpho says, 'I loved the start. The middle was a bit fast — try slower.' What kind of feedback is this?
options: Balanced and helpful — both positive and improvement, specific
questions.expected: Balanced and helpful — both positive and improvement, specific
questions.memo: Specific praise + specific improvement = balanced feedback. Lerato can use it.

questions.question: When a friend gives you feedback you don't like, the WORST thing to do is:
questions.ruby_prompt: When a friend gives you feedback you don't like, what's the worst thing to do?
options: Attack them or stop being their friend
questions.expected: Attack them or stop being their friend
questions.memo: Attacking the messenger ends friendships and stops people from telling you anything true. Lonely place.

questions.question: Karabo gets feedback from her teacher, her mother and her friend. Should they all agree?
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo gets feedback from her teacher, her mom and her friend. Will they all agree?
options: Maybe not — different people notice different things
Only one of them is right
questions.expected: Maybe not — different people notice different things
questions.memo: Different people see different sides. The pattern across many people's feedback is what matters more than any one piece.

questions.question: True or false: Saying 'thank you' is a good way to end receiving feedback, even if you disagree.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Saying 'thank you' is a good way to end receiving feedback, even if you disagree.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — thanks acknowledges the effort the other person made. You can still decide later what to do with the feedback.

questions.question: Which feedback is SPECIFIC enough to act on?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which feedback is specific enough that the person could actually act on it?
options: 'Your second paragraph needs an example to support the point.'
questions.expected: 'Your second paragraph needs an example to support the point.'
questions.memo: Specific feedback points to the exact place AND the exact fix. Vague feedback ('bad', 'try harder') doesn't help.

questions.question: Why might an adult sometimes give feedback that feels hard?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why might an adult give feedback that feels hard to hear?
options: Because they want you to grow and they see what you can become
questions.expected: Because they want you to grow and they see what you can become
questions.memo: Loving adults often see our potential more clearly than we do. Their hard feedback usually comes from belief in us, not from cruelty.

LS.L5.PSW.T03.title: Coping with emotions
LS.L5.PSW.T03.description: Empathy, compassion, anger, disappointment and sadness. Skills to manage emotions positively; the significance of friends in times of sadness, tragedy and change.
LS.L5.PSW.T03.recovery_strategy: Normalise all emotions; focus on healthy ways to express them. If a learner shares a tough feeling, validate first, then offer practical coping ideas.

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the word 'empathy' mean?
options: Understanding and sharing how someone else feels
questions.expected: Understanding and sharing how someone else feels
questions.memo: Empathy is feeling alongside someone — putting yourself in their shoes. It's a key skill for friendship.

questions.question: What is 'compassion'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is compassion?
options: Caring about someone's pain and wanting to help
questions.expected: Caring about someone's pain and wanting to help
questions.memo: Compassion takes empathy one step further — not just feeling with them but wanting to help.

questions.question: Sipho's grandmother passed away. He feels deep sadness. This feeling is called:
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho's grandmother passed away. The deep sadness he feels has a name. What is it?
questions.expected: Grief
questions.memo: Grief is the deep sadness of losing someone we love. It comes in waves and is normal.

questions.question: What is 'disappointment'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is disappointment?
options: The feeling when something doesn't go the way you hoped
questions.expected: The feeling when something doesn't go the way you hoped
questions.memo: Disappointment comes when our hopes meet a different reality. It's normal and can teach us to hope wisely.

questions.question: Which is a HEALTHY way to manage anger?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a healthy way to manage anger?
options: Walk away, breathe slowly, then talk about it
questions.expected: Walk away, breathe slowly, then talk about it
questions.memo: Healthy anger management: walk away from the trigger, calm the body (breath, water, movement), then use words.

questions.question: True or false: All feelings are okay to have, even unpleasant ones.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: All feelings are okay to have, even the hard ones.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — feelings aren't right or wrong. What matters is what we DO with them. Anger is okay; hitting isn't.

questions.question: Lerato's friend's parent died. The most important thing Lerato can do is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato's friend's parent has died. What's the most important thing Lerato can do?
options: Be there — listen, hug, sit quietly. She doesn't need to 'fix' it
Tell her friend to stop crying
Tell jokes to cheer her up
questions.expected: Be there — listen, hug, sit quietly. She doesn't need to 'fix' it
questions.memo: Grieving people don't need fixing or cheering — they need someone to BE with them. Presence beats words.

questions.question: Why are friends so important during sad times?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are friends so important when something sad happens?
options: They remind us we are not alone and care about us
questions.expected: They remind us we are not alone and care about us
questions.memo: Sadness feels lighter when shared. A friend who listens — even without saying anything — gives huge comfort.

questions.question: Which is a way to manage SADNESS in a healthy way?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a healthy way to manage sadness?
options: Talk to someone you trust and let yourself cry if you need to
questions.expected: Talk to someone you trust and let yourself cry if you need to
questions.memo: Sadness needs to be felt and shared, not buried. Talking to a trusted person and letting tears come is healthy.

questions.question: Mpho is angry because her brother broke her toy. The healthy first step is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho is angry because her brother broke her toy. What's the healthy first step?
options: Take a few deep breaths before saying anything
questions.expected: Take a few deep breaths before saying anything
questions.memo: Breath before action calms the body. Once calm, words are much more powerful than fists or tears.

questions.question: When a friend is grieving, you should NOT say:
questions.ruby_prompt: When a friend is grieving, which of these is NOT a kind thing to say?
options: 'I am so sorry. I'm here for you.'
questions.expected: 'Just get over it.'
questions.memo: 'Get over it' rushes grief. Grief takes time. The other three sentences all show real support.

questions.question: Karabo doesn't make the school netball team. She feels disappointed. A healthy response is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo doesn't make the school netball team. She is disappointed. What's a healthy response?
options: Let herself feel sad, then plan more practice for next time
Tell everyone she didn't want to be in it anyway
questions.expected: Let herself feel sad, then plan more practice for next time
questions.memo: Disappointment hurts. Feeling it briefly, then deciding on the next move is the path of growth.

questions.question: Put these steps in order for calming down a strong feeling.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order for calming down when a strong feeling hits.
options: Notice the feeling and name it (anger, fear, sadness)
Move your body — walk, breathe, drink water
Talk to a friend or trusted adult
Decide what to do once you're calm
questions.expected: Notice the feeling and name it (anger, fear, sadness),Move your body — walk, breathe, drink water,Talk to a friend or trusted adult,Decide what to do once you're calm
questions.memo: Name → move → connect → decide. Name-it-to-tame-it is real — naming a feeling shrinks its power.

questions.question: Tell me one thing you do that helps you feel calmer when you're upset.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing you do that helps you feel calmer when you're upset.
questions.expected: I take deep breaths and count to ten
questions.memo: Good answers: deep breaths, walk outside, drink water, talk to mom/dad, draw, listen to music, hug a pet, run. Find yours and use it.

questions.question: Which shows EMPATHY?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these shows empathy?
options: 'I can see this is really hard for you.'
questions.expected: 'I can see this is really hard for you.'
questions.memo: Empathy names the other person's feelings out loud. It says 'I see you' more than 'I have a fix'.

questions.question: True or false: A big change (like moving home) can bring many feelings at once.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: A big change like moving home can bring many feelings at once.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — big changes bring excitement, fear, sadness, hope, all mixed. All those feelings are normal.

questions.question: Sipho feels his anger building. What's a quick on-the-spot tool?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho can feel his anger building up. What's a quick tool he can use on the spot?
options: Slow deep breaths — in for 4, out for 6
Yell as loud as he can
questions.expected: Slow deep breaths — in for 4, out for 6
questions.memo: Slow breathing calms the nervous system fast. Longer out-breath than in-breath is the trick. Works in seconds.

questions.question: When a feeling is too big to handle alone, the BEST step is:
questions.ruby_prompt: When a feeling is too big to handle alone, what's the best step?
options: Tell a trusted adult — a parent, teacher, counsellor — or call Childline 116
questions.expected: Tell a trusted adult — a parent, teacher, counsellor — or call Childline 116
questions.memo: Asking for help is brave, not weak. Childline 116 is free in SA and listens to any worry.

questions.question: Which is a sign your friend might need support?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these might be a sign your friend needs your support?
options: They become very quiet, don't play, look tired and sad
questions.expected: They become very quiet, don't play, look tired and sad
questions.memo: Big changes in behaviour can mean someone is struggling inside. Notice the change and gently check in.

questions.question: What's the difference between empathy and sympathy?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the difference between empathy and sympathy?
options: Empathy = feeling WITH someone. Sympathy = feeling sorry FOR them.
questions.expected: Empathy = feeling WITH someone. Sympathy = feeling sorry FOR them.
questions.memo: Empathy joins in: 'I get it, I've felt that too.' Sympathy is gentler but more distant: 'Sorry that's happening to you.' Both are kind; empathy goes deeper.

LS.L5.PSW.T04.title: Relationships with peers, older people and strangers
LS.L5.PSW.T04.description: Safe and unsafe relationships, bad and good relationships, benefits of good and safe relationships.
LS.L5.PSW.T04.recovery_strategy: Affirm the learner's instincts — if something feels wrong, it usually is. Reinforce trusted-adult paths. Be calm and matter-of-fact about stranger safety.

questions.question: What is a 'peer'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a peer?
options: Someone about the same age as you
questions.expected: Someone about the same age as you
questions.memo: Peers are people roughly your age. Classmates, friends in your grade, kids at your sports club — all peers.

questions.question: Which is a GOOD relationship?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a good relationship?
options: One where both people respect, listen and care about each other
One where one person bosses the other
questions.expected: One where both people respect, listen and care about each other
questions.memo: Good relationships have respect, kindness, honesty and care that goes both ways.

questions.question: Which is a sign of a BAD or unsafe relationship?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a sign of a bad or unsafe relationship?
options: The person makes you feel scared, hurt or controlled
The person treats you with respect
questions.expected: The person makes you feel scared, hurt or controlled
questions.memo: Fear, hurt, control — these are big warning signs. Healthy relationships build us up, not break us down.

questions.question: What is a 'stranger'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a stranger?
questions.expected: A person you don't know
questions.memo: A stranger is someone you don't know. Most strangers are harmless, but you treat unknown people with extra care.

questions.question: A stranger offers you sweets and a ride. The right answer is:
questions.ruby_prompt: A stranger offers you sweets and a ride. What's the right answer?
options: Say no, walk away to a safe place, and tell a trusted adult
Take the ride but leave the sweets
questions.expected: Say no, walk away to a safe place, and tell a trusted adult
questions.memo: Never go anywhere with a stranger, even for sweets or 'help' they ask. Get to a safe place and tell a trusted adult quickly.

questions.question: True or false: A grown-up should NEVER ask a child for help finding a lost dog or directions.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: A grown-up should never ask a child for help finding a lost dog or directions.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Adults ask other ADULTS for help — not lone children. If an adult tries this, it's a warning sign. Walk away and tell a trusted adult.

questions.question: What's a 'safe relationship' with an older person (an adult)?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a safe relationship with an older person — an adult — look like?
options: They listen, respect your boundaries, and don't ask you to keep secrets
They want to be alone with you a lot
They make you keep secrets from your parents
questions.expected: They listen, respect your boundaries, and don't ask you to keep secrets
questions.memo: Safe adults respect your no, your privacy, and don't isolate you or ask for secrets. The other options are warning signs.

questions.question: An adult tells you 'this is our special secret — don't tell anyone'. You should:
questions.ruby_prompt: An adult says 'this is our special secret — don't tell anyone'. What should you do?
options: Tell a parent or trusted adult straight away
questions.expected: Tell a parent or trusted adult straight away
questions.memo: Safe adults don't ask kids to keep secrets from their parents. This is one of the biggest warning signs. Tell another trusted adult fast.

questions.question: A good friend would NOT:
questions.ruby_prompt: A good friend would NOT do which of these?
options: Make fun of you in front of others to look cool
Stand up for you when others are mean
questions.expected: Make fun of you in front of others to look cool
questions.memo: Real friends don't tear you down to look good. If a 'friend' often does, that relationship needs to change.

questions.question: Which is a BENEFIT of having good relationships?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a benefit of having good relationships in your life?
options: You feel safer, happier and able to ask for help when you need it
questions.expected: You feel safer, happier and able to ask for help when you need it
questions.memo: Good relationships build a safety net. People with strong relationships handle life's hard moments better.

questions.question: Lerato's older neighbour gives her gifts and asks her not to tell her mom. What should Lerato do?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato's older neighbour gives her gifts and tells her not to tell her mom. What should Lerato do?
options: Tell her mom right away — this is not a safe pattern
questions.expected: Tell her mom right away — this is not a safe pattern
questions.memo: Adults using gifts + secrecy to build a special bond with a child = warning. Telling mom protects Lerato.

questions.question: Which of these helps build a GOOD friendship?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these helps build a good friendship?
options: Honesty, listening, and being there in good and hard times
questions.expected: Honesty, listening, and being there in good and hard times
questions.memo: Good friendships are built on honest words and reliable presence. Gifts and gossip don't last.

questions.question: True or false: It's okay to say no to an adult if they're asking you to do something that feels wrong.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: It's okay to say no to an adult if they're asking you to do something that feels wrong.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — even adults can be wrong. Your gut feeling about safety matters. Say no, get to safety, tell a trusted grown-up.

questions.question: Karabo is walking home alone. A car slows down beside her and the driver smiles. What should she do?
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo is walking home alone. A car slows beside her and the driver smiles. What should she do?
options: Walk fast in the opposite direction and toward people or a shop
Wave back and keep walking past
questions.expected: Walk fast in the opposite direction and toward people or a shop
questions.memo: Cars can't easily turn around. Walking the opposite way buys safety. Heading toward people or a shop adds witnesses and help.

questions.question: Tell me one thing a TRUSTED ADULT in your life does that makes them trustworthy.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing a trusted adult in your life does that makes them trustworthy.
questions.expected: They listen to me without judging
questions.memo: Good answers: listens, keeps me safe, doesn't shout, helps me, tells me the truth, doesn't ask me to keep secrets from other safe adults.

questions.question: Put these in order for what to do if a stranger tries to talk to you alone.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order for what to do if a stranger tries to talk to you when you're alone.
options: Move to where there are people
Walk or run to a safe person (shop owner, police, parent)
Tell a trusted adult about it
questions.expected: Don't get close to them,Move to where there are people,Walk or run to a safe person (shop owner, police, parent),Tell a trusted adult about it
questions.memo: Distance → people → safe adult → tell. This sequence has saved many children.

questions.question: A friend keeps copying your homework and never gives anything back. This is a:
questions.ruby_prompt: A friend keeps copying your homework and never gives anything back. This is a sign of:
options: An unfair relationship — friendships go both ways
questions.expected: An unfair relationship — friendships go both ways
questions.memo: Healthy friendships are reciprocal — both people give and receive. One-sided is a sign something is wrong.

questions.question: Mpho's friend pushes her to do things she's not comfortable with. The healthy response is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho's friend keeps pushing her to do things she's not comfortable with. What's the healthy response?
options: Say no clearly, and talk to a trusted adult if pushing continues
Just do everything the friend says
questions.expected: Say no clearly, and talk to a trusted adult if pushing continues
questions.memo: Real friends respect your no. If a friend keeps pushing past your no, they're not respecting you — that's not a friendship to keep.

questions.question: Which is the BEST description of a safe adult in your life?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the best description of a safe adult in your life?
options: Someone who listens, respects your no, and won't ask you to keep secrets from other trusted adults
Someone who buys you the most things
questions.expected: Someone who listens, respects your no, and won't ask you to keep secrets from other trusted adults
questions.memo: Safe adults are not defined by gifts, age or job. They're defined by HOW they treat you — with respect, openness and no harmful secrets.

questions.question: Why do good relationships matter for your health?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do good relationships matter for your health?
options: People with good relationships are happier, sleep better and even live longer
questions.expected: People with good relationships are happier, sleep better and even live longer
questions.memo: Decades of research show strong relationships protect mental and physical health. Friendships are not just nice — they're medicine.

LS.L5.PSW.T05.title: Discrimination, stereotype and bias
LS.L5.PSW.T05.description: Concepts of discrimination, stereotype and bias as violations of children's rights; how to protect self and others, where to find help, planning a response in own local context.
LS.L5.PSW.T05.recovery_strategy: Define terms simply with everyday examples. Affirm that all people deserve equal treatment under the SA Constitution.

questions.question: What is 'discrimination'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does discrimination mean?
options: Treating someone unfairly because of who they are (race, language, religion, etc.)
questions.expected: Treating someone unfairly because of who they are (race, language, religion, etc.)
questions.memo: Discrimination is unfair treatment based on race, gender, religion, language, disability and other parts of identity. It's against the SA Constitution.

questions.question: What is a 'stereotype'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a stereotype?
options: A fixed idea about a group of people that may not be true of individuals
questions.expected: A fixed idea about a group of people that may not be true of individuals
questions.memo: Stereotypes are 'all X people are like Y'. They make individuals invisible. Real people are always more than the group they belong to.

questions.question: What is 'bias'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is bias?
options: Leaning toward or away from something or someone unfairly
questions.expected: Leaning toward or away from something or someone unfairly
questions.memo: Bias is an unfair lean — favouring one side or person over another without good reason. We can have biases without even noticing.

questions.question: Which is an example of discrimination?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is an example of discrimination?
options: A child is refused entry to a club because of the colour of their skin
A child wins a prize for hard work
questions.expected: A child is refused entry to a club because of the colour of their skin
questions.memo: Refusing entry because of skin colour is racial discrimination — and against the SA Constitution. Fair access for all is the rule.

questions.question: Which is an example of a STEREOTYPE?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a stereotype?
questions.expected: 'Boys don't cry'
questions.memo: 'Boys don't cry' is a fixed idea about a whole group (boys). The other options are observations about specific things, not stereotypes.

questions.question: True or false: Discrimination is a violation of children's rights.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Discrimination is a violation of children's rights.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — every child has the right to be treated equally under the SA Constitution. Discriminating against a child breaks that right.

questions.question: Sipho hears a classmate use a racist word about another child. What should he do?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho hears a classmate use a racist word about another child. What should he do?
options: Tell the classmate that's not okay and tell a teacher
questions.expected: Tell the classmate that's not okay and tell a teacher
questions.memo: Speaking up against racism is powerful. Telling a teacher means an adult can deal with it properly.

questions.question: Which document in SA protects everyone from discrimination?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which big document in South Africa protects everyone from discrimination?
options: The Constitution and the Bill of Rights
questions.expected: The Constitution and the Bill of Rights
questions.memo: The Bill of Rights is part of the SA Constitution. It says everyone is equal and protects us from unfair discrimination.

questions.question: A bias can be:
questions.ruby_prompt: A bias can be:
options: Either positive (favouring) or negative (disliking) without good reason
questions.expected: Either positive (favouring) or negative (disliking) without good reason
questions.memo: Bias can go either way — favouring people like you OR disliking those who aren't. Both are bias.

questions.question: Lerato says: 'Girls can't play football.' This is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato says, 'Girls can't play football.' What is this?
options: A stereotype — many girls and women play football well
questions.expected: A stereotype — many girls and women play football well
questions.memo: Banyana Banyana (the SA women's national football team) and many others prove this stereotype wrong. People are bigger than the boxes society draws.

questions.question: If you see another child being discriminated against, you can:
questions.ruby_prompt: If you see another child being discriminated against, what can you do?
options: Stand by them, tell an adult, and don't join the discriminating
questions.expected: Stand by them, tell an adult, and don't join the discriminating
questions.memo: Bystanders make a huge difference. Standing with the person, telling an adult, refusing to join in — all help.

questions.question: True or false: Everyone has SOME biases — even kind people.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Everyone has some biases — even kind people.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: We all soak up ideas from family, media and society. The work isn't to be free of bias — it's to notice it and challenge it in ourselves.

questions.question: Karabo is told she 'can't be a scientist because she's a girl'. The truth is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo is told she can't be a scientist because she's a girl. What's the truth?
options: Girls and women can and do become scientists in every field
questions.expected: Girls and women can and do become scientists in every field
questions.memo: Many of the world's top scientists are women — and SA has its own famous women scientists like Quarraisha Abdool Karim. Stereotypes are not facts.

questions.question: Where can a child in SA find help if their rights are being violated?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where can a child in South Africa find help if their rights are being violated?
options: Childline 116, a school counsellor, the SA Human Rights Commission, or a trusted adult
Only the school principal can help
questions.expected: Childline 116, a school counsellor, the SA Human Rights Commission, or a trusted adult
questions.memo: Help is real and free. Childline 116 (24-hour), school counsellor, SAHRC (rights body), and any trusted adult are all paths.

questions.question: Put these steps in order if you experience discrimination at school.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these steps in order if you experience discrimination at school.
options: Notice what happened and how it made you feel
Tell a teacher or counsellor you trust
Ask for it to be dealt with — there are school policies
Talk to a parent or Childline if it continues
questions.expected: Notice what happened and how it made you feel,Tell a teacher or counsellor you trust,Ask for it to be dealt with — there are school policies,Talk to a parent or Childline if it continues
questions.memo: Notice → tell → ask for action → escalate. Every step makes the next easier.

questions.question: Tell me one example of a stereotype you have heard.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one stereotype you have heard about a group of people.
questions.expected: Boys don't cry
questions.memo: Good answers: any 'all X are Y' statement — 'boys are tough', 'girls like pink', 'old people are slow', etc. Once we notice a stereotype, we can challenge it.

questions.question: Which is a way to PROTECT yourself and others from discrimination?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a way to protect yourself and others from discrimination?
options: Learn the Bill of Rights, speak up kindly, and ask trusted adults for help
Make fun of those who report it
questions.expected: Learn the Bill of Rights, speak up kindly, and ask trusted adults for help
questions.memo: Knowing your rights gives you confidence to act. Calm speaking-up + adult help beats silence or revenge.

questions.question: Why is the apartheid history important to know when learning about discrimination in SA?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is apartheid history important to know when learning about discrimination in SA?
options: South Africa lived through extreme legal discrimination — knowing this helps us never go back
questions.expected: South Africa lived through extreme legal discrimination — knowing this helps us never go back
questions.memo: Apartheid was a system of racial discrimination by law. Remembering it — and the people who ended it — helps SA stay watchful and united.

questions.question: Which is a positive action a class can take to reduce discrimination at school?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a positive action a class can take to reduce discrimination at school?
options: Make a class promise to speak up when discrimination happens
Form separate groups by race or language
questions.expected: Make a class promise to speak up when discrimination happens
questions.memo: Class agreements set a culture. When the whole class promises to speak up, individuals feel braver. Cultures shift this way.

questions.question: The most powerful answer to discrimination is:
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the most powerful answer to discrimination?
options: Treating every person as equal in dignity and worth
questions.expected: Treating every person as equal in dignity and worth
questions.memo: Equal dignity is the heart of the SA Constitution and of Ubuntu. Living it every day is the strongest answer.

LS.L5.PSW.T06.title: Child abuse
LS.L5.PSW.T06.description: Forms of child abuse (physical and emotional), effects on personal health, strategies to deal with abuse, where to get help and report abuse.
LS.L5.PSW.T06.recovery_strategy: Always reinforce: abuse is NEVER the child's fault. Telling a trusted adult or Childline 116 is the bravest, smartest move. Never describe abuse in graphic terms.

questions.question: What is 'child abuse'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is child abuse?
options: When a grown-up or older person hurts a child on purpose — physically or emotionally
When a child loses a sports match
questions.expected: When a grown-up or older person hurts a child on purpose — physically or emotionally
questions.memo: Child abuse is on-purpose harm to a child — hitting, hurting, scaring, or threatening. It is against the law and against children's rights.

questions.question: Which is a form of PHYSICAL abuse?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a form of physical abuse?
options: Hitting, shaking or burning a child
Asking a child to wash dishes
Asking a child to make their bed
questions.expected: Hitting, shaking or burning a child
questions.memo: Physical abuse is using the body to hurt — hitting, slapping, kicking, shaking, burning. Chores and homework are normal childhood, not abuse.

questions.question: Which is a form of EMOTIONAL abuse?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a form of emotional abuse?
options: Repeatedly insulting, scaring or rejecting a child
Telling a child you love them
questions.expected: Repeatedly insulting, scaring or rejecting a child
questions.memo: Emotional abuse is using words and actions to crush a child's spirit — repeated put-downs, threats, isolation, or being told they're unwanted.

questions.question: True or false: Child abuse is NEVER the child's fault.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Child abuse is never the child's fault.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Always true. Children are never to blame for being abused. Abuse is the responsibility of the abuser, not the child.

questions.question: Where can a child in South Africa call to report abuse, for free, day or night?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where can a child in South Africa call to report abuse — free, day or night?
questions.expected: Childline 116
questions.memo: Childline 116 is free from any phone in SA. Trained counsellors listen and help. They can also help with police or social workers.

questions.question: If a child is being abused, the most important first step is:
questions.ruby_prompt: If a child is being abused, what's the most important first step?
options: Tell a trusted adult (teacher, neighbour, parent of a friend) or call Childline 116
questions.expected: Tell a trusted adult (teacher, neighbour, parent of a friend) or call Childline 116
questions.memo: Telling breaks the silence that keeps abuse going. There are people whose JOB it is to help — telling them is brave, not wrong.

questions.question: Effects of abuse on personal health can include:
questions.ruby_prompt: Effects of abuse on a child's personal health can include what?
options: Trouble sleeping, sadness, fear, and physical harm
questions.expected: Trouble sleeping, sadness, fear, and physical harm
questions.memo: Abuse hurts the whole child — body, sleep, feelings, school. With help and care, healing is possible. That's why telling matters.

questions.question: A friend tells you they are being hurt at home and asks you not to tell. You should:
questions.ruby_prompt: A friend tells you they are being hurt at home but asks you not to tell anyone. What should you do?
options: Tell a trusted adult anyway — this is one secret that protecting saves lives
questions.expected: Tell a trusted adult anyway — this is one secret that protecting saves lives
questions.memo: Real friendship is keeping your friend safe — even if they're scared of telling. A trusted adult or Childline can help both of you.

questions.question: True or false: When a child tells about abuse, they should be believed and helped.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: When a child tells about abuse, they should be believed and helped.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Children almost never make up abuse. Believing a child who speaks up is the start of helping them.

questions.question: Which is a TRUSTED ADULT a child could tell about abuse?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which adult could a child tell about abuse?
options: A teacher, school counsellor, family doctor, religious leader, or a friend's parent
Only their own parents (even if a parent is the abuser)
questions.expected: A teacher, school counsellor, family doctor, religious leader, or a friend's parent
questions.memo: Trusted adults are everywhere. If the abuse is at home, the adult to tell is NOT at home — try a teacher, counsellor or friend's parent.

questions.question: Sipho's older cousin keeps slapping him when no one is looking. What should Sipho do?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho's older cousin keeps slapping him when no one is looking. What should Sipho do?
options: Tell a parent, teacher or call Childline 116 — this is abuse
Wait for the cousin to grow up
questions.expected: Tell a parent, teacher or call Childline 116 — this is abuse
questions.memo: Hitting a child IS abuse — even from family. Sipho deserves safety. Telling brings the help that stops the cycle.

questions.question: Put these steps in order for what to do if you are being abused.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these steps in the right order for what to do if you are being abused.
options: Get to a safe place if you can
Tell a trusted adult or call Childline 116
Look after yourself with the help of caring grown-ups
questions.expected: Get to a safe place if you can,Tell a trusted adult or call Childline 116,Keep telling until someone helps,Look after yourself with the help of caring grown-ups
questions.memo: Safety → tell → keep telling → heal. Sometimes the first adult doesn't act — KEEP TELLING. Help is real.

questions.question: Which sentence is TRUE about abuse?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is true about abuse?
options: Abuse happens in all kinds of families — rich or poor, big or small
questions.expected: Abuse happens in all kinds of families — rich or poor, big or small
questions.memo: Abuse crosses every line of money, race, religion and language. That's why every child needs to know how to ask for help.

questions.question: Karabo is being abused by an adult at home. She is scared to tell. The most important thing she needs to know is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo is being abused by an adult at home. She's scared to tell. What's the most important thing she needs to know?
options: It is not her fault, she is not alone, and there are adults whose JOB is to help her
questions.expected: It is not her fault, she is not alone, and there are adults whose JOB is to help her
questions.memo: Three truths bigger than the fear: not your fault, not alone, real help exists. Hold onto them. Call Childline 116 (free).

questions.question: True or false: Insults and threats are abuse, even when nobody hits anyone.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Insults and threats are abuse, even when nobody is hit.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Emotional abuse (constant insults, threats, rejection) is real abuse. Children deserve emotional safety too.

questions.question: Tell me a phone number a child in SA can call for help with abuse.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me a phone number a child in South Africa can call for help with abuse.
questions.expected: 116 — Childline South Africa
questions.memo: Childline 116. Free. 24 hours. Trained to listen and help. Memorise this number — it can save a friend's life one day.

questions.question: If the first adult you tell doesn't help, you should:
questions.ruby_prompt: If the first adult you tell doesn't help, you should:
options: Tell another trusted adult — and another, until someone helps
questions.expected: Tell another trusted adult — and another, until someone helps
questions.memo: Some adults react badly to hard news. That's on them, not you. KEEP telling. The right help is out there.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT abuse — it's normal childhood?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is NOT abuse — it's just normal childhood?
options: Being asked to help with chores at home
Being hit hard until you bruise
questions.expected: Being asked to help with chores at home
questions.memo: Chores are normal. Hitting, daily shouting and isolation are abuse. The difference is harm vs ordinary family life.

questions.question: Mpho hears a child scream in pain next door, regularly. What should Mpho do?
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho hears a child scream in pain next door regularly. What should Mpho do?
options: Tell a parent or teacher — they can report it to a social worker
questions.expected: Tell a parent or teacher — they can report it to a social worker
questions.memo: When you hear repeated screams of pain, a child may need help. Telling an adult can save that child. Social workers can step in.

questions.question: What is the SAFEST first thing to remember if you are being abused?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the safest first thing to remember if you are being abused?
options: You are not alone, it is not your fault, and there is real help — Childline 116
questions.expected: You are not alone, it is not your fault, and there is real help — Childline 116
questions.memo: These four words can change a life: not alone, not my fault, real help. Repeat them. Call Childline 116. Tell.

LS.L5.PSW.T07.title: Dealing with violent situations
LS.L5.PSW.T07.description: Identifying potential violent situations at home, school and community; responding effectively; ways to avoid and protect oneself, where to find help.
LS.L5.PSW.T07.recovery_strategy: Priority is always GET AWAY SAFELY, not confront. Reinforce: telling a trusted adult or police is the right action. Don't romanticise being brave.

questions.question: What is a 'violent situation'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a violent situation?
options: A situation where someone might or does get physically hurt
questions.expected: A situation where someone might or does get physically hurt
questions.memo: Violent situations are where harm to bodies could happen — fights, attacks, hijackings, robberies, abuse.

questions.question: When you see a fight starting, the SAFEST first thing is:
questions.ruby_prompt: When you see a fight starting, what's the safest first thing to do?
options: Get away to a safe place — don't try to break it up yourself
questions.expected: Get away to a safe place — don't try to break it up yourself
questions.memo: Untrained people who jump in often get hurt too. Safety first. Then tell an adult who can stop it properly.

questions.question: If someone tries to take your phone or bag on the street, the safest move is:
questions.ruby_prompt: If someone tries to take your phone or bag on the street, what is the safest move?
options: Give it up — your safety is worth more than any object
questions.expected: Give it up — your safety is worth more than any object
questions.memo: Things can be replaced. You cannot. Police agree: hand it over, get to safety, and report it.

questions.question: Where can you usually find help in a public place during a violent situation?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where can you usually find help in a public place when something violent is happening?
options: A shop, a police station, a security guard, or a busy place with many people
questions.expected: A shop, a police station, a security guard, or a busy place with many people
questions.memo: People = safety. Empty places = danger. Run toward where there are witnesses and adults.

questions.question: What is the SA police emergency number?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the SA police emergency number?
questions.memo: 10111 = SA Police. 10177 = ambulance. 112 from a mobile phone connects to emergency services. Worth memorising.

questions.question: True or false: It is brave to fight any attacker by yourself.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: It is brave to fight any attacker by yourself.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: Movies make it look brave; real life makes it dangerous. Getting away and getting help is the wise move.

questions.question: At home, if you hear adults fighting violently, the safest place for a child is:
questions.ruby_prompt: At home, if adults are fighting violently, where is the safest place for a child?
options: Go to a safe room or neighbour, and call a trusted adult or Childline 116
Try to break up the fight
Hide in the middle of it
questions.expected: Go to a safe room or neighbour, and call a trusted adult or Childline 116
questions.memo: Children must NEVER try to break up adult fights. Get to a safe space — locked room, neighbour, outside — and call for help.

questions.question: Lerato sees a robbery happening across the street. What should she do?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato sees a robbery happening across the street. What should she do?
options: Move away to safety and call 10111 or tell an adult to call
questions.expected: Move away to safety and call 10111 or tell an adult to call
questions.memo: Witnesses can describe what happened to police later. But first, safety. Move away. Then call.

questions.question: Which is a way to AVOID being in a violent situation?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a way to avoid being in a violent situation?
options: Walk in groups, in busy streets, and during the day when possible
Walk alone late at night in quiet places
Wear loose jewellery as a target
questions.expected: Walk in groups, in busy streets, and during the day when possible
questions.memo: Most crime targets the vulnerable — alone, dark places, late hours. Group + busy + daylight is the safer mix.

questions.question: If you witness violence at school, you should:
questions.ruby_prompt: If you witness violence at school, what should you do?
options: Tell a teacher or principal immediately
questions.expected: Tell a teacher or principal immediately
questions.memo: Teachers can stop violence faster than children can. Telling = action. Watching = the violence continues.

questions.question: True or false: Carrying a weapon to protect yourself is the best response.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Carrying a weapon at school to protect yourself is the best response.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: Weapons at school are dangerous and illegal. They often make children targets and get used against them. Safety = adults + plans + avoiding hot spots.

questions.question: Put these in order for what to do if you're attacked.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order for what to do if you are attacked.
options: Move toward people or a safe place
Tell a trusted adult or call 10111
Talk to a counsellor afterwards about your feelings
questions.expected: Give up belongings if asked,Move toward people or a safe place,Tell a trusted adult or call 10111,Talk to a counsellor afterwards about your feelings
questions.memo: Give up stuff → get safe → report → process feelings. The whole sequence matters, including the emotional part.

questions.question: Karabo's neighbourhood has a lot of violence. The best thing for her family to do is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo's neighbourhood has a lot of violence. What's the best thing her family can do?
options: Plan safe routes, keep doors locked, know neighbours, and contact community safety groups
questions.expected: Plan safe routes, keep doors locked, know neighbours, and contact community safety groups
questions.memo: Plans, locked doors, friendly neighbours, community watch — these layers add up to real safety in tough areas.

questions.question: Sipho is being asked to join a gang. What should he do?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho is being asked to join a gang. What should he do?
options: Say no, tell a trusted adult, and stay close to safe friends
questions.expected: Say no, tell a trusted adult, and stay close to safe friends
questions.memo: Gangs lead to violence, prison, and death. Saying no is the only safe answer. A trusted adult or social worker can help with the pressure.

questions.question: Tell me one safety rule for walking to school.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one safety rule for walking to school.
questions.expected: Walk with friends, not alone
questions.memo: Good answers: walk in groups, use main routes, tell a parent the route, don't talk to strangers, carry only what's needed, look up not at a phone.

questions.question: Mpho sees a gun on the floor at her school. What should she do?
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho sees a gun on the floor at her school. What should she do?
options: Don't touch it. Move away. Tell a teacher straight away
questions.expected: Don't touch it. Move away. Tell a teacher straight away
questions.memo: Guns hurt and kill — even by 'accident'. Don't touch. Move away. Get an adult. That sequence saves lives.

questions.question: After a frightening event, it's normal to feel:
questions.ruby_prompt: After a frightening or violent event, it's normal to feel what?
options: Shaken, scared, sad or angry for some time afterwards — talking to a counsellor helps
questions.expected: Shaken, scared, sad or angry for some time afterwards — talking to a counsellor helps
questions.memo: Strong feelings after a scare are normal — your body and mind processing it. School counsellors and Childline (116) can help.

questions.question: Which sign warns that a situation might get violent?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which sign might warn that a situation could get violent?
options: People shouting, threatening or fists clenched
questions.expected: People shouting, threatening or fists clenched
questions.memo: Early warning signs: raised voices, threats, fists, blocked exits, alcohol involved. Notice them and move away early.

questions.question: Why is it important to talk to someone after a violent event?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it important to talk to someone after a violent event?
options: Sharing helps you process the fear and stops it from getting stuck
questions.expected: Sharing helps you process the fear and stops it from getting stuck
questions.memo: Untalked-about fear can linger for years. A counsellor or trusted adult helps the feelings move through, not stay stuck.

questions.question: What's the MOST IMPORTANT rule about violent situations?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the most important rule about violent situations?
options: Get yourself to safety first, then get help — things can be replaced; you cannot
Always try to be a hero
questions.expected: Get yourself to safety first, then get help — things can be replaced; you cannot
questions.memo: Safety first, help second. This rule is from real police and rescuers. Your life is worth more than any object or moment of pride.

LS.L5.PSW.T08.title: Issues of age and gender in cultural contexts
LS.L5.PSW.T08.description: Relationships between elders and children in different SA cultural contexts; responsibilities of boys and girls; contributions of women and men.
LS.L5.PSW.T08.recovery_strategy: Respect cultural traditions while affirming the SA Constitution's equality. Help the learner see both: the value of elders' wisdom AND the equal dignity of girls and boys.

questions.question: In many SA cultures, what is shown to elders (older people)?
questions.ruby_prompt: In many South African cultures, what is shown to elders?
options: Respect — they are seen as keepers of wisdom and tradition
questions.expected: Respect — they are seen as keepers of wisdom and tradition
questions.memo: Across SA cultures, elders are valued for life experience and as guides for younger generations.

questions.question: Which is a way to show respect to an elder?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these shows respect to an elder?
options: Greeting them first and listening when they speak
questions.expected: Greeting them first and listening when they speak
questions.memo: Greeting elders first, using respectful titles ('mama', 'tata', 'baba'), and listening — all show respect.

questions.question: True or false: Boys and girls have equal rights under the SA Constitution.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Boys and girls have equal rights under the SA Constitution.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — the SA Constitution guarantees gender equality. Girls and boys may do the same jobs and have the same chances in life.

questions.question: Which is a stereotype about gender?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a gender stereotype?
options: 'Some girls play rugby and some don't'
questions.expected: 'Girls don't play rugby'
questions.memo: Banning girls from a sport based on gender is a stereotype. The Springbok Women prove it's untrue.

questions.question: Which is a stereotype about boys?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a stereotype about boys?
questions.expected: 'Boys don't cook'
questions.memo: Many world-famous chefs are men. The stereotype that boys don't cook is just that — a stereotype.

questions.question: In SA, MEN and WOMEN can do which kinds of work?
questions.ruby_prompt: In South Africa, which kinds of work can men and women do?
options: The same kinds — there are female doctors, engineers, taxi drivers; male nurses, teachers, chefs
There are completely separate jobs by gender
questions.expected: The same kinds — there are female doctors, engineers, taxi drivers; male nurses, teachers, chefs
questions.memo: SA has women presidents in business and government, women miners, male nurses and teachers. The Constitution opened all work to all people.

questions.question: Name a South African woman who has contributed greatly to the country:
questions.ruby_prompt: Name a South African woman who has contributed greatly to the country.
options: Winnie Madikizela-Mandela, Albertina Sisulu, Charlotte Maxeke
Only foreign women have done this
questions.expected: Winnie Madikizela-Mandela, Albertina Sisulu, Charlotte Maxeke
questions.memo: Many SA women have shaped our country — in freedom struggle, science, business, sports. Knowing their names matters.

questions.question: Which is a way an ELDER can teach a younger person?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a way an elder can teach a younger person?
options: Telling stories from their life and the past
questions.expected: Telling stories from their life and the past
questions.memo: Stories carry wisdom. Many African cultures pass on lessons through grandparents' and parents' stories.

questions.question: True or false: Both boys and girls can take part in chores at home.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Both boys and girls can take part in chores at home.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Cooking, cleaning, fetching water, looking after younger siblings — these are family tasks, not 'girl' or 'boy' tasks.

questions.question: In some traditional homes, what is the SHARED responsibility of all children?
questions.ruby_prompt: In many traditional SA homes, what's a shared responsibility of all children?
options: Respecting elders, helping with family tasks, doing well at school
questions.expected: Respecting elders, helping with family tasks, doing well at school
questions.memo: Across SA cultures, children share these core duties — respect, help, learn. Specific tasks may vary, but the values overlap.

questions.question: Lerato wants to be an engineer. Her grandmother says, 'That's a man's job.' What's true?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato wants to become an engineer. Her grandmother says, 'That's a man's job.' What is true?
options: South Africa has many women engineers — Lerato can absolutely become one
questions.expected: South Africa has many women engineers — Lerato can absolutely become one
questions.memo: Times have changed. Many SA women are engineers, scientists, surgeons. Lerato can pursue her dream — and respect her grandmother while doing so.

questions.question: Why is it important to learn FROM elders?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it important to learn from elders?
options: They've lived through things we can learn from without making the same mistakes
questions.expected: They've lived through things we can learn from without making the same mistakes
questions.memo: Elders' life experience is a free gift to younger people. They've seen droughts, wars, freedom, change — wisdom that books can't fully capture.

questions.question: Karabo's brother says girls 'shouldn't be loud or strong'. What's the truth?
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo's brother says girls 'shouldn't be loud or strong.' What's the truth?
options: Girls can be loud or quiet, strong or gentle — whatever they choose, just like boys
questions.expected: Girls can be loud or quiet, strong or gentle — whatever they choose, just like boys
questions.memo: Personality is personal — not a gender rule. Some girls are quiet, some loud; same for boys. All are okay.

questions.question: Which is a healthy view of age and gender in SA?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a healthy view of age and gender in SA?
options: Respect for elders + equal rights for all genders
questions.expected: Respect for elders + equal rights for all genders
questions.memo: We can hold both: respect tradition AND uphold equality. The SA Constitution and Ubuntu both make space for these together.

questions.question: Tell me one task at home that BOTH boys and girls can do.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one task at home that both boys and girls can do.
questions.expected: Washing dishes
questions.memo: Good answers: washing dishes, sweeping, cooking, looking after siblings, doing laundry, gardening. Any home task can be shared.

questions.question: Sipho's class is told 'only boys lift the heavy tables'. What's a fairer rule?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho's class is told 'only boys lift the heavy tables.' What would be fairer?
options: Anyone strong enough can help — not based on gender
questions.expected: Anyone strong enough can help — not based on gender
questions.memo: Strength varies between individuals, not whole genders. A fair rule asks for help by ability, not gender.

questions.question: When younger and older family members work together, the result is often:
questions.ruby_prompt: When younger and older family members work together, what's the result often?
options: Both learn — young get wisdom, elders get help and new ideas
questions.expected: Both learn — young get wisdom, elders get help and new ideas
questions.memo: Inter-generational work is two-way. Grandchildren learn ancient skills; grandparents learn technology. Both grow.

questions.question: True or false: Men can be loving caregivers to children too.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Men can be loving caregivers to children too.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Fathers, uncles, grandfathers, male teachers — men nurture children every day. It's part of being human.

questions.question: What's a respectful way to disagree with an elder?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a respectful way to disagree with an elder?
options: Listen first, ask questions, then share your view calmly
questions.expected: Listen first, ask questions, then share your view calmly
questions.memo: Respect and disagreement can live together. Listen, ask, share — that pattern keeps the relationship strong.

questions.question: The SA Constitution says about gender:
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the SA Constitution say about gender?
options: Everyone is equal regardless of gender — no discrimination is allowed
questions.expected: Everyone is equal regardless of gender — no discrimination is allowed
questions.memo: Section 9 of the Constitution forbids unfair discrimination on the basis of gender. Everyone is equal before the law.

LS.L5.PSW.T09.title: Festivals and customs of religions in South Africa
LS.L5.PSW.T09.description: Festivals and customs from a variety of religions in South Africa.
LS.L5.PSW.T09.recovery_strategy: Treat each festival with equal respect. Aim is recognition and curiosity, not deep theology. Use SA examples where possible.

questions.question: What is a 'religious festival'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a religious festival?
options: A special celebration that is part of a religion
questions.expected: A special celebration that is part of a religion
questions.memo: Religious festivals are special days that follow a faith's calendar — celebrating events, people or seasons that matter to the religion.

questions.question: Christmas is a major festival for which religion?
questions.ruby_prompt: Christmas is a major festival for which religion?
questions.expected: Christianity
questions.memo: Christmas — 25 December — celebrates the birth of Jesus in Christianity. Many SA Christians attend church services and gather with family.

questions.question: Eid is a festival for which religion?
questions.ruby_prompt: Eid is a festival for which religion?
questions.expected: Islam
questions.memo: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan (a month of fasting). Eid al-Adha celebrates Abraham. SA Muslims celebrate both with prayers and family meals.

questions.question: Diwali (the Festival of Lights) is celebrated by:
questions.ruby_prompt: Diwali — the Festival of Lights — is celebrated by which religion?
questions.expected: Hindus
questions.memo: Diwali is the Hindu Festival of Lights — symbolising light over darkness. KZN's Hindu communities celebrate with lamps, sweets and prayer.

questions.question: Passover (Pesach) is celebrated by:
questions.ruby_prompt: Passover, also called Pesach, is celebrated by which religion?
questions.expected: Jewish people
questions.memo: Passover remembers the Israelites' escape from slavery in Egypt. SA Jewish families gather for a special Seder meal with traditional foods.

questions.question: True or false: SA has many religions and many religious festivals throughout the year.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: South Africa has many religions and many religious festivals throughout the year.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — SA is religiously rich. Major festivals come from Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Judaism, Buddhism and African Religion across the year.

questions.question: Ramadan is a special month in Islam when Muslims:
questions.ruby_prompt: Ramadan is a special month in Islam when Muslims:
options: Fast from food and drink during daylight hours
questions.expected: Fast from food and drink during daylight hours
questions.memo: During Ramadan, adult Muslims don't eat or drink from dawn to sunset. It's a time of prayer, charity and self-discipline.

questions.question: Easter, in Christianity, celebrates:
questions.ruby_prompt: Easter, in Christianity, celebrates what?
questions.expected: The resurrection of Jesus
questions.memo: Easter (in March or April) is the most important Christian festival — the resurrection of Jesus after his death. Many SA Christians attend church services.

questions.question: Vesak (Wesak) is a festival celebrated by:
questions.ruby_prompt: Vesak, sometimes called Wesak, is a festival of which religion?
questions.expected: Buddhists
questions.memo: Vesak celebrates the birth, enlightenment and death of the Buddha. Buddhists often light lanterns and gather for meditation.

questions.question: African Religion includes ceremonies to:
questions.ruby_prompt: African Religion includes ceremonies to do what?
options: Honour ancestors and important life events
questions.expected: Honour ancestors and important life events
questions.memo: Ancestor ceremonies — for births, deaths, marriages, illness, milestones — are central in African Religion across SA.

questions.question: Why do many religions celebrate festivals?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do many religions celebrate festivals?
options: To remember important events and share them with family and community
questions.expected: To remember important events and share them with family and community
questions.memo: Festivals carry memory, story and belonging. They link generations and strengthen community.

questions.question: When a classmate is fasting for Ramadan, you can show respect by:
questions.ruby_prompt: When a classmate is fasting for Ramadan, you can show respect by:
options: Not making a big show of eating in front of them and asking what helps them
Eating extra food in front of them
Pretending to fast yourself when you're not
questions.expected: Not making a big show of eating in front of them and asking what helps them
questions.memo: Small kindnesses go a long way — being quiet about your own food, asking what they need. Respect doesn't require sharing the belief.

questions.question: True or false: Knowing about other religions' festivals helps us live together better.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Knowing about other religions' festivals helps us live together better.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — understanding our neighbours' celebrations builds bridges. SA's strength is in its diversity.

questions.question: Hanukkah, the Jewish Festival of Lights, is celebrated by:
questions.ruby_prompt: Hanukkah, the Jewish Festival of Lights, is celebrated by lighting what?
options: A menorah — a nine-branched candleholder, over eight nights
A single candle for one hour
questions.expected: A menorah — a nine-branched candleholder, over eight nights
